'''unearth''' (un-ėrth′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''earth''.] '''1.''' To drive or bring forth from an earth or burrow; drive from any underground hole or burrow; draw from the earth.
{{smaller block|<poem>A rough terrier of the hills;
By birth and call of nature pre-ordained
To hunt the badger and ''unearth'' the fox.</poem>
{{right|''Wordsworth'', Prelude, iv.}}}}
'''2.''' To uncover from the earth; dig out of the ground; exhume, as fossils; exfodiate.
{{smaller block|To ''unearth'' the root of an old tree.
{{right|''Wordsworth'', Simon Lee.}} moonlight nights which belong to Italy.
{{right|''Aldrich'', Ponkapog to Pesth, p. 31.}}}}

'''uneasiness''' (un-ē′zi-nes), ''n.'' The state of being uneasy; want of ease or comfort, physical or mental. ''Shak.'', Hen. V., ii. 2. 27.

'''uneasy''' (un-ē′zi), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not easy either in body or in mind; feeling some lack of ease, either mental or physical; disturbed; unquiet.
{{smaller block|''Uneasy'' lies the head that wears a crown.
{{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. IV., iii. 1. 31.}}}}
'''2.''' Not easy or elegant in manner or style; not graceful; constrained; stiff; awkward. {{smaller block|Shall I live at Home a stiff melancholy poor Man of Quality, grow ''uneasy'' to my Acquaintance as well as myself, by fancying I’m slighted where I am not?
{{right|''Steele'', Grief A-la-Mode, ii. 1.}}}}
'''3.''' Causing pain, trouble, constraint, discomfort, or want of ease; cramping; constraining; irksome; disagreeable.
{{smaller block|The waies were exceeding ''uneasie''. For they were wonderfull hard. {{right|''Coryat'', Crudities, I. 92.}}}}
{{smaller block|He puts a force and constraint upon himself which is ''uneasie'' to any man, and he lets the vizard fall off sometimes when it is more observed than he thinks.
{{right|''Stillingfleet'', Sermons, II. v.}}}}
{{smaller block|This account was very ''uneasy'' to me.
{{right|''T. Ellwood'', Life (ed. Howells), p. 220.}}}}
{{smaller block|Walpole had, it is plain, an ''uneasy'' consciousness of the frivolity of his favourite pursuits.
{{right|''Macaulay'', Horace Walpole.}}}}
'''4.''' Not easy to be done or accomplished; difficult.
{{smaller block|<poem>But this swift business
I must ''uneasy'' make, lest too light winning
Make the prize light. ''Shak.'', Tempest, i. 2. 451.</poem>}}

'''uneatable''' (un-ē′ta̤-bl), ''a.'' Not eatable; not fit to be eaten: as, ''uneatable'' fruit.
{{smaller block|Big scarlet hips—which are ''uneatable'' by us.
{{right|''Grant Allen'', Colin Clout’s Calendar, p. 119.}}}}

'''uneatableness''' (un-ē′ta̤-bl-nes), ''n.'' The quality or state of being uneatable. ''Wallace'', Natural Selection, iii. 120.

'''uneaten''' (un-ē′tn), ''a.'' Not eaten; not devoured; hence, not destroyed.
{{smaller block|Therefore I will out-swear him and all his followers, that this is all that ’s left ''uneaten'' of my sword.
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', King and No King, iii.}}}}

'''uneath''' (un-ēᴛ̵ʜ′), ''a.'' [< ME. ''unethe'', ''onethe'', < AS. ''uneáthe'', difficult, < ''un-'', not, + ''eáthe'', easy: see ''un-''<sup>1</sup> and ''eath'', ''a.''] Not easy; difficult. [Obsolete or archaic.]
{{smaller block|''Uneath'' it were to tell.
{{right|''Southey.''}}}}

'''uneath†''' (un-ēᴛ̵ʜ′), ''adv.'' [< ME. ''unethe'', ''uneth'', ''unnethe'', ''unneth'', ''onethe'', ''onnethe'', etc., < AS. ''uneáthe'', not easily, < ''un-'', not, + ''eáthe'', easily: see ''eath'', ''adv.'' Cf. ''uneaths''.] Not easily; hardly; scarcely.
{{smaller block|<poem>Atte last a forster came rideng;
And, wete ye wele, so sorrowfull he was
That he ''onnethe'' myght speke to the kyng.</poem>
{{right|''Generydes'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 977.}}
''Uneath'' may she endure the flinty street.
{{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. VI., ii. 4. 8.}}}}
